drills.q: What is SR 26-2, when was it issued, and what two prior SR letters did it rescind and replace?
drills.a: SR 26-2, issued jointly by the Fed, OCC, and FDIC on April 17, 2026, is the revised interagency guidance on Model Risk Management. It supersedes and replaces SR 11-7 (April 2011, governed for 15 years) and SR 21-8 (2021, BSA/AML-specific MRM guidance).

drills.q: State SR 26-2's three-prong test for what counts as a 'model' and give an example of something newly excluded.
drills.a: (1) Complex quantitative method/system, (2) applies statistical/economic/financial theory, (3) processes inputs into quantitative estimates. Excludes simple arithmetic/spreadsheets and deterministic rule engines without underlying theory -- e.g. a spreadsheet summing a fixed fee schedule against a fixed rate table is no longer formally an inventory-worthy model, though a spreadsheet implementing a regression-derived pricing adjustment still qualifies.

drills.q: Why does SR 26-2 explicitly exclude generative AI, RAG, and agentic AI from its formal model scope, and what's the practical risk of over-reading that exclusion?
drills.a: The agencies cite these technologies as 'novel and rapidly evolving,' deliberately avoiding premature, quickly-obsolete binding rules. The practical risk: an agentic AI system that can move money or influence a lending decision carries real prudential/reputational risk regardless of its formal categorization, and examiners scrutinize AI governance broadly in practice even absent a binding rule -- 'not formally a model' does not mean 'no governance needed.'

drills.q: Walk through the three pillars of model validation and identify which is hardest to execute for a deep learning model versus a logistic regression.
drills.a: Conceptual soundness (design/assumptions appropriate for use), outcomes analysis (backtesting/benchmarking), ongoing monitoring (performance holds up post-deployment). Conceptual soundness is hardest for deep learning: a regression's coefficients and economic rationale are directly inspectable, but a neural network/GBM ensemble has no equivalent closed form -- review must shift to architecture justification, training-data provenance, and evaluation-harness design.

drills.q: What changed about validation frequency between SR 11-7 and SR 26-2, and why doesn't removing blanket annual revalidation necessarily mean less rigor?
drills.a: SR 11-7 practice defaulted to routine, often-annual revalidation regardless of materiality. SR 26-2 reframes frequency as a function of materiality, change velocity, and data availability with explicit re-review triggers. A high-materiality, high-change-velocity model (e.g. a continuously retrained fraud model) should actually see MORE frequent review under this scheme than a fixed annual calendar gave it; the risk is only in poor implementation, not the design intent.

drills.q: Define 'effective challenge' and explain how SR 26-2 strengthened it, including the org-design implication for a Chief Model Risk Officer.
drills.a: Effective challenge requires model review to be genuinely independent and critical, with real authority to force changes, not a rubber-stamp. SR 26-2 requires independent reviewers to have genuine organizational standing and authority to halt deployment when risk is unmitigated. Implication: MRM leadership needs a real seat at the model-deployment decision table with escalation/veto authority to executive management, not an advisory sign-off a business line can override.

drills.q: Explain SR 26-2's materiality-based tiering formula and the specific monitoring capability its 'detect when a model becomes material' requirement forces engineering teams to build.
drills.a: Materiality = model exposure ($ magnitude of decisions) x model purpose (regulatory-critical vs internal) x inherent risk. High-materiality gets intensive oversight; immaterial gets light controls PROVIDED an automated mechanism exists to detect materiality growth. This forces live, ongoing usage/exposure tracking for every registered model (not a one-time launch assessment) with automatic re-tiering triggers, since a model can scale from a small pilot to material scope over time.

drills.q: Why doesn't an LLM hallucination map cleanly onto the traditional input/specification/estimation/use-error model-risk taxonomy?
drills.a: That taxonomy assumes a model with legible internal logic and separable failure causes. A hallucination isn't clearly an input error (the prompt can be entirely correct), a specification error (no small set of assumptions to inspect), or a discrete implementation bug -- it behaves more like an emergent property of a probabilistic generative process interacting with an underspecified evaluation surface, requiring supplementary LLM-specific categories (hallucination, prompt-injection, guardrail-bypass, training-data provenance risk).

drills.q: What happened before SR 11-7, and what specific 2008-crisis failure directly motivated it?
drills.a: Before 2011, model risk was handled ad hoc within individual business lines with no unified firm-wide standard or mandated independent validation function. The 2008 crisis exposed this: deeply flawed mortgage-related valuation/rating models (MBS/CDO pricing and the ratings built on them) had no independent, empowered effective-challenge process forcing critical review before driving trillions of dollars of exposure. SR 11-7 (April 4, 2011) was the Fed/OCC's direct response.

drills.q: Design question: you're asked to build MRM-equivalent governance for a new agentic AI system that can autonomously initiate wire transfers, even though SR 26-2 formally excludes agentic AI from scope. What do you build, and how do you argue for the investment if leadership says it isn't legally required?
drills.a: Build proportional to actual business risk: inventory entry with exposure tracking (authority limit x transaction frequency), independent red-teaming for prompt-injection/unauthorized-action/guardrail-bypass, ongoing drift/anomaly monitoring, and a real effective-challenge mechanism with authority to pause the system. Argue on prudential/reputational-risk grounds independent of the regulatory carve-out -- reframe from 'compliance' to 'operational risk control for an autonomous system with financial authority,' the same segregation-of-duties and audit controls already required for a human employee with wire-transfer authority apply with equal force to a non-human agent with the same authority.
